summary.en: Venezuela disclosed a $237.5 billion debt pile and moved forward with a large restructuring while the United States signed a security cooperation pact with the interim Venezuelan government, after which a U.S. marine died falling overboard during a Caribbean operation linked to the renewed ties. The Senate is probing JD Vance for allegedly steering a Venezuelan oil license to Vitol and another senator’s role in the same deal, while Citi weighs a market re-entry after a five-year exit. Venezuelan authorities later declared the security pact null and void, illegal gold mining continues, and Eni and Repsol pledged a $2 billion joint-venture investment. According to UCDP, there were 2 battle-related deaths in 2007.
summary.nb: Venezuela offentliggjorde en gjeld på $237.5 milliarder og gikk videre med en omfattende restrukturering mens USA signerte en sikkerhetssamarbeidsavtale med den midlertidige venezuelanske regjeringen, hvoretter en amerikansk marine døde etter å ha falt overbord under en karibisk operasjon knyttet til de fornyede båndene. Senatet etterforsker JD Vance for påstått å ha styrt en venezuelansk oljelisens til Vitol og en annen senators rolle i samme avtale, mens Citi vurderer en gjeninntreden i markedet etter en fem-års exit. Venezuelanske myndigheter erklærte senere sikkerhetsavtalen ugyldig, ulovlig gullgruvedrift fortsetter, og Eni og Repsol lovet en fellesinvestering på $2 milliarder. Ifølge UCDP var det 2 kamprelaterte dødsfall i 2007.

background.title: Crisis in Venezuela
background.extract: An ongoing socioeconomic and political crisis began in Venezuela during the presidencies of Hugo Chávez, Nicolás Maduro as well as Delcy Rodríguez. It has been marked by hyperinflation, starvation, disease, crime, and mortality rates, resulting in massive emigration. Food shortages and hyperinflation have ended, but inflation remains high. It is the worst economic crisis in Venezuela's history and considered by some sources as more severe than the Great Depression in the United States, the 1985–1994 Brazilian economic crisis, or the 2008–2009 hyperinflation in Zimbabwe. In 2019, the Institute of International Finance called it the single largest economic collapse outside of war in 45 years. Writers have compared aspects, such as unemployment and GDP contraction, to Bosnia and Herzegovina after the 1992–95 Bosnian War, and those in Russia, Cuba and Albania following the Revolutions of 1989.
